title: Building APIs with FastAPI
description: REST fundamentals for AI apps, FastAPI routes and Pydantic models, async endpoints, and request validation.

lessons.title: REST Fundamentals for AI Apps
lessons.description: Turning a model that works in a notebook into something another program can actually call.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Apply the resource-and-HTTP-verb conventions from the Software Engineering course specifically to an endpoint that wraps a model call.

sections.title: 🔌 The gap this course closes
sections.content: Every model built earlier in this curriculum — a fine-tuned classifier, a RAG pipeline, an agent — exists as Python code you can call directly. A real product needs that logic reachable over the network, with a stable contract, from a web app, a mobile app, or another service. That's the gap this course exists to close.

sections.title: 🌐 Modeling an AI operation as a resource
sections.content: A chat completion becomes `POST /conversations/{id}/messages`, a document upload for RAG becomes `POST /documents`, and a fine-tuning job becomes a resource you can `GET /jobs/{id}` to check status on — applying the resource-based API design principles from the Software Engineering course directly to AI-specific operations.

sections.title: ⏱️ Why AI endpoints break some ordinary API assumptions
sections.content: A typical REST endpoint responds in milliseconds; an LLM call can take seconds, and a fine-tuning job can take hours. This single fact — that AI operations are often slow relative to typical API responses — is the reason this course dedicates entire modules to streaming (Module 2) and background jobs (Module 3) that a typical CRUD API tutorial doesn't need to cover.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's the resource-modeling idea made concrete: an AI operation represented as a resource with its own URL, rather than a single "do the thing" endpoint.

```python
# --- The wrong shape: one endpoint that tries to do everything synchronously ---

def bad_generate_endpoint(prompt):
    """POST /generate -- blocks until the whole model call finishes, no way to check status."""
    return call_model(prompt)  # could take 30+ seconds; the client just waits

# --- The resource-based shape: the job itself is a resource you can query ---

jobs = {}
next_job_id = 1

def call_model(prompt):
    return f"response to: {prompt}"

def post_jobs(prompt):
    """POST /jobs -- returns immediately with a resource the client can check later."""
    global next_job_id
    job_id = next_job_id
    next_job_id += 1
    jobs[job_id] = {"id": job_id, "status": "completed", "result": call_model(prompt)}
    return 201, jobs[job_id]

def get_job(job_id):
    """GET /jobs/{id} -- the same resource, checked on the client's own schedule."""
    if job_id not in jobs:
        return 404, {"error": "not found"}
    return 200, jobs[job_id]

status, body = post_jobs("summarize this document")
print(status, body)
status, body = get_job(body["id"])
print(status, body)
```

`bad_generate_endpoint` bakes the action into a single call the client has to sit through. `post_jobs` and `get_job` instead treat the operation as a resource — creation returns a `201` with the job's own identity, and that same identity can be queried again later with `GET /jobs/{id}`, exactly the pattern the lesson describes for a fine-tuning job.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Designing one endpoint per action instead of one resource with HTTP verbs.** `/generateSummary`, `/checkJobStatus`, `/cancelJob` as three separate ad hoc endpoints duplicate what `POST /jobs`, `GET /jobs/{id}`, and `DELETE /jobs/{id}` already express through the resource plus the HTTP method.

**Assuming every AI endpoint can respond as fast as a typical CRUD endpoint.** Designing the API contract around a same-request, instant-response assumption works until the first LLM call or fine-tuning job that takes longer than a client is willing to wait.

**Forgetting that the gap this course closes is a real engineering gap, not a formality.** A model that only runs in a notebook isn't a product yet — the network-reachable, stable-contract version of it is genuinely different work, not a thin wrapper.

questions.question: What real-world gap does this course's opening lesson identify?
options: The gap between a model that works as Python code and a stable, network-reachable API another program can call
The gap between training and evaluation datasets
The gap between two different embedding models
The gap between SQL and NoSQL databases
questions.explanation: Turning working model code into something callable over a network with a stable contract is exactly the product-engineering gap this course addresses.

questions.question: Why does modeling a fine-tuning job as a resource (`GET /jobs/{id}`) make sense?
options: Because it follows the same resource-based API design principles from the Software Engineering course, applied to a long-running AI operation
Because fine-tuning jobs cannot be represented as resources under any API convention
Because GET requests are required to trigger fine-tuning
Because job status can only be checked through a database query, never an API
questions.explanation: Treating the job itself as a resource you can query status on directly extends the general resource-modeling principle to an AI-specific, long-running operation.

questions.question: Why do AI-specific API endpoints often break the 'responds in milliseconds' assumption of a typical REST tutorial?
options: Because LLM calls and fine-tuning jobs can take seconds to hours, unlike typical fast CRUD operations
Because AI endpoints never return any response at all
Because REST cannot be used for any AI-related endpoint
Because AI models always respond faster than database queries
questions.explanation: The comparatively long duration of real AI operations is exactly why this course needs dedicated modules on streaming and background jobs that a standard CRUD API wouldn't require.

questions.question: In the code example, what does `post_jobs` return, and why is that shape better than `bad_generate_endpoint`?
options: It returns the finished result only, identical to bad_generate_endpoint
It returns a 201 status and the job resource itself, including its id, so the client can query it again later via get_job
It returns nothing and silently discards the result
It returns a 500 error every time
questions.explanation: `post_jobs` returns `201, jobs[job_id]`, giving the client the job's identity as a resource — exactly what lets `get_job` retrieve the same job again later, unlike `bad_generate_endpoint`'s one-shot blocking call.

questions.question: What does `get_job` return if called with a `job_id` that was never created?
options: 200 and an empty dictionary
404 and {'error': 'not found'}
It raises an unhandled exception
201 and a newly created job
questions.explanation: `get_job` explicitly checks `if job_id not in jobs` and returns `404, {"error": "not found"}` rather than crashing or fabricating a result.

questions.question: Why is designing three separate ad hoc endpoints like `/generateSummary`, `/checkJobStatus`, and `/cancelJob` flagged as a mistake?
options: Because it's technically impossible to implement
Because it duplicates what a single resource (`/jobs`) combined with different HTTP verbs already expresses
Because ad hoc endpoint names are always shorter to type
Because it violates a hard limit on the number of endpoints an API can have
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes point out that action-named endpoints re-invent what resource-plus-verb design (`POST /jobs`, `GET /jobs/{id}`, `DELETE /jobs/{id}`) already covers more consistently.

questions.question: Why is assuming every AI endpoint can respond as fast as a typical CRUD endpoint a mistake?
options: Because it works fine as an assumption until an LLM call or fine-tuning job takes longer than a client will wait
Because CRUD endpoints are always slower than AI endpoints
Because AI endpoints never take more than a few milliseconds
Because this assumption has no bearing on API design
questions.explanation: The lesson explains this assumption breaks down specifically because AI operations can be genuinely slow, which is exactly why streaming and background jobs get dedicated modules later in the course.

questions.question: Why does the lesson describe a notebook-only model as 'not a product yet'?
options: Because notebooks cannot run Python code
Because making it network-reachable with a stable contract is genuinely different engineering work, not a thin wrapper
Because models in notebooks are always less accurate
Because products cannot use Python at all
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes emphasize that the gap between notebook code and a real, network-reachable API is a substantive engineering gap, which is exactly what this course is built to close.

lessons.title: FastAPI Basics: Routes and Models
lessons.description: A concrete Python framework for building the APIs described in the last lesson.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Describe how FastAPI defines routes and validates request/response data using type-annotated models.

sections.title: 🛣️ Routes: mapping a URL and method to a function
sections.content: FastAPI maps an HTTP method and path to a Python function using decorators — `@app.post("/documents")` calls a specific function whenever a POST request arrives at that path, with FastAPI handling the parsing of the request into Python objects automatically based on type hints.

sections.title: 📐 Pydantic models define the data contract
sections.content: Instead of manually checking that a request body has the right fields and types, FastAPI uses Pydantic models — Python classes with type-annotated fields — to define exactly what a valid request or response looks like. A request that doesn't match the model's shape is automatically rejected with a clear error, before your business logic ever runs.

sections.title: 📄 Automatic documentation, as a side effect
sections.content: Because routes and models are defined with type hints, FastAPI can automatically generate interactive API documentation (via OpenAPI/Swagger) with no extra work — directly addressing the API-documentation need flagged in the Software Engineering course's API design lesson, essentially for free.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Pydantic's validation is the part worth seeing fail on purpose — here's a model rejecting a malformed payload before any route logic runs.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

class DocumentUpload(BaseModel):
    title: str
    content: str
    max_chunk_size: int = 500  # has a default, so it's optional

# --- A valid request: parses cleanly ---

good_payload = {"title": "Q3 Report", "content": "Revenue grew...", "max_chunk_size": 300}
doc = DocumentUpload(**good_payload)
print("parsed:", doc)

# --- A malformed request: missing a required field ---

bad_payload = {"title": "Q3 Report"}  # 'content' is missing entirely

try:
    DocumentUpload(**bad_payload)
except ValidationError as e:
    print("rejected before any route logic ran:")
    for err in e.errors():
        print(f"  {err['loc']}: {err['msg']}")

# --- A wrong-type request: max_chunk_size isn't an int ---

wrong_type_payload = {"title": "Q3 Report", "content": "...", "max_chunk_size": "not a number"}
try:
    DocumentUpload(**wrong_type_payload)
except ValidationError as e:
    print("also rejected:", e.errors()[0]["msg"])
```

`good_payload` parses into a `DocumentUpload` instance with no fuss. `bad_payload` is missing the required `content` field, so Pydantic raises a `ValidationError` naming exactly which field is missing — this is the automatic rejection the lesson describes, happening before any of your own route code runs. `wrong_type_payload` shows the same thing for a type mismatch: `max_chunk_size` is declared as `int`, so a string value is rejected too.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Skipping Pydantic models and manually checking `request.json()` fields by hand.** This re-implements, less reliably, exactly what a type-annotated model already gives you automatically, and it's easy to miss a field or a type check that Pydantic would have caught by default.

**Treating the automatic docs as optional polish.** Because the documentation is generated directly from the same type hints that drive validation, it stays in sync with the actual contract for free — skipping it means writing (and maintaining) documentation manually for something FastAPI already produces correctly.

**Giving every field a default value just to avoid validation errors.** A field that's actually required (like `content` for a document upload) should stay required — defaulting it to an empty string just moves a missing-data bug from an immediate, clear validation error to a confusing failure somewhere downstream.

questions.question: How does FastAPI map an incoming HTTP request to a specific Python function?
options: Through decorators that associate an HTTP method and path with a function, like `@app.post("/documents")`
By reading a separate XML configuration file for every route
By requiring all requests to use the GET method exclusively
By manually parsing the raw request string inside every function body
questions.explanation: FastAPI's decorator syntax directly ties a route definition to the function that should handle requests matching that path and method.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a Pydantic model in a FastAPI route?
options: To define the exact expected shape of request/response data, so invalid requests are rejected automatically before business logic runs
To store the application's database connection settings
To render the final HTML response to the client
To replace the need for any HTTP methods entirely
questions.explanation: Pydantic models act as a validation contract, catching malformed requests automatically based on the model's type-annotated fields.

questions.question: Why does FastAPI's automatic API documentation matter, connecting back to the Software Engineering course?
options: It directly satisfies the need for clear API documentation flagged in the earlier API design lesson, essentially for free from existing type hints
Because documentation is otherwise impossible to produce for any API
Because FastAPI requires documentation to be written manually in a separate tool
Because automatic documentation replaces the need for request validation
questions.explanation: The type-hint-driven approach means documentation stays in sync with the actual code, directly addressing a concern raised earlier in the curriculum about API contracts.

questions.question: In the code example, what happens when `DocumentUpload(**bad_payload)` is called with `bad_payload = {"title": "Q3 Report"}`?
options: It parses successfully with content set to an empty string
It raises a ValidationError because the required 'content' field is missing
It silently ignores the missing field
It crashes with an unrelated TypeError
questions.explanation: `content` has no default value in `DocumentUpload`, so omitting it causes Pydantic to raise a `ValidationError` naming the missing field, exactly the automatic rejection the lesson describes.

questions.question: Why does `good_payload` parse successfully while `wrong_type_payload` does not?
options: Because good_payload provides all required fields with correct types, while wrong_type_payload provides max_chunk_size as a string instead of an int
Because wrong_type_payload is missing the title field
Because good_payload uses a completely different model class
There is no actual difference between the two payloads
questions.explanation: `good_payload` matches the model's declared types exactly, while `wrong_type_payload` supplies a string for `max_chunk_size`, which is type-annotated as `int`, triggering a `ValidationError`.

questions.question: Why is manually checking `request.json()` fields by hand instead of using a Pydantic model flagged as a mistake?
options: Because it's faster than using Pydantic
Because it re-implements, less reliably, validation that a type-annotated model already provides automatically
Because manual checks are required by FastAPI
Because Pydantic models cannot validate JSON data
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes point out that hand-rolled field checking duplicates what Pydantic validation already does, with a higher risk of missing a field or type check Pydantic would have caught by default.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against treating FastAPI's automatic documentation as optional polish?
options: Because the documentation is generated from the same type hints that drive validation, so skipping it means manually maintaining something that's otherwise free and automatically in sync
Because automatic documentation is always inaccurate
Because documentation has no connection to an API's actual contract
Because FastAPI charges extra for documentation generation
questions.explanation: Because the docs come directly from the type hints already written for validation, treating them as skippable polish throws away documentation that's otherwise correct and free.

questions.question: Why is giving every field a default value just to avoid validation errors called a mistake?
options: Because default values are not supported in Pydantic
Because it turns a genuinely required field's missing-data bug from an immediate, clear validation error into a confusing failure further downstream
Because default values always slow down request parsing
Because fields with defaults cannot be type-checked
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that defaulting an actually-required field (like content) just to dodge a validation error trades a clear, immediate error for a harder-to-diagnose problem later in the pipeline.

lessons.title: Async Endpoints and Background Tasks
lessons.description: Why an API that calls an LLM shouldn't block a whole worker thread while it waits.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain why async endpoints matter specifically for I/O-bound operations like LLM API calls.

sections.title: ⏳ The problem: waiting is wasted capacity
sections.content: A traditional synchronous endpoint that calls an external LLM API blocks its entire worker thread for the whole duration of that call — often several seconds — during which that worker can't handle any other request. At any real traffic volume, this wastes enormous capacity waiting on network I/O rather than doing useful computation.

sections.title: ⚡ Async: doing something else while waiting
sections.content: An async endpoint (defined with `async def` in FastAPI) can yield control back to the event loop while waiting on an I/O operation like an LLM API call, letting the same worker handle other requests during that wait — dramatically improving how many concurrent requests a single process can serve, since most of an LLM call's latency is spent waiting on the network, not on local computation.

sections.title: 🔧 Background tasks: fire, respond, then finish the work
sections.content: For work that doesn't need to complete before responding to the client — like logging an interaction or triggering a downstream notification — FastAPI's background tasks let you return a response immediately while the task finishes after, avoiding making the client wait for work they don't need to wait for.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
A simulated event loop makes the difference between blocking and yielding concrete without needing a real server.

```python
import time

# --- Synchronous: one slow call blocks everything behind it ---

def sync_call_llm(request_id, delay):
    print(f"[sync] request {request_id}: blocking for {delay}s")
    time.sleep(delay)  # simulates waiting on the network for an LLM response
    return f"response-{request_id}"

start = time.perf_counter()
for req_id, delay in [(1, 0.05), (2, 0.05), (3, 0.05)]:
    sync_call_llm(req_id, delay)
sync_elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"sync total: {sync_elapsed:.3f}s (roughly 3 * 0.05s, one after another)")

# --- Async: overlapping waits, using asyncio.gather ---

import asyncio

async def async_call_llm(request_id, delay):
    print(f"[async] request {request_id}: awaiting for {delay}s")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)  # yields control back to the event loop while waiting
    return f"response-{request_id}"

async def run_concurrently():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        async_call_llm(1, 0.05),
        async_call_llm(2, 0.05),
        async_call_llm(3, 0.05),
    )
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f"async total: {elapsed:.3f}s (roughly 0.05s, all three overlapped)")
    return results

asyncio.run(run_concurrently())
```

The synchronous version calls `sync_call_llm` three times in a row, so the total time is roughly the sum of all three delays (about 0.15s). The async version instead awaits all three with `asyncio.gather`, so while each one is waiting on `asyncio.sleep` (standing in for the network wait on an LLM call), the event loop can make progress on the others — the total time is roughly the *longest* single delay (about 0.05s), not the sum, which is exactly the capacity win the lesson describes.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Marking a route `async def` but still calling a blocking library inside it.** An `async def` endpoint that calls a synchronous, blocking HTTP client still blocks the event loop for that call's full duration — declaring a function async doesn't make the code inside it non-blocking by itself; the I/O calls inside it need to actually be awaited async calls.

**Using a background task for work the client actually needs the result of.** If the client's next action depends on the task's output, firing it as a background task and returning early just moves the problem — the client ends up polling or guessing when the real answer is ready instead of getting it directly.

**Assuming async automatically makes CPU-bound work faster.** Async helps specifically with I/O-bound waiting, like a network call to an LLM API. It does nothing for a slow, CPU-bound computation running in the same process, which still blocks the event loop regardless of how the function is declared.

questions.question: Why does a synchronous endpoint calling an LLM API waste server capacity at scale?
options: Because it blocks its entire worker thread for the whole duration of the call, preventing that worker from handling any other request meanwhile
Because synchronous endpoints cannot call external APIs at all
Because LLM APIs only accept asynchronous requests
Because blocking calls always use more CPU than async calls
questions.explanation: The worker sits idle waiting on network I/O rather than doing useful work, which compounds badly under real concurrent traffic.

questions.question: What does an async endpoint do differently while waiting on an LLM API call?
options: It yields control back to the event loop, letting the same worker handle other requests during the wait
It creates an entirely new server process for every request
It blocks all other requests until the LLM call completes, same as a synchronous endpoint
It skips calling the LLM API entirely
questions.explanation: Yielding control during I/O wait is exactly what lets a single async worker serve many concurrent requests efficiently.

questions.question: When is a FastAPI background task the right tool to use?
options: When work doesn't need to complete before responding to the client, like logging or triggering a downstream notification
When the client must wait for the task's result before receiving any response
Only for tasks that take less than one millisecond
Only for tasks that call an LLM directly
questions.explanation: Background tasks let the response return immediately while non-blocking follow-up work completes afterward, avoiding unnecessary client wait time.

questions.question: In the code example, roughly how long does the synchronous version take to process all three requests?
options: Roughly 0.05s, since all three run at once
Roughly the sum of all three delays, about 0.15s, since each call happens one after another
Roughly 0s, since sync calls are instant
It never completes
questions.explanation: `sync_call_llm` is called three times in a plain loop, each one fully blocking with `time.sleep(delay)` before the next starts, so the total is roughly the sum of the three 0.05s delays.

questions.question: Why does the async version's total time come out closer to 0.05s instead of 0.15s?
options: Because asyncio.gather runs all three async_call_llm calls concurrently, so their waits overlap instead of stacking up
Because async code always skips the delay entirely
Because only one of the three calls actually executes
Because asyncio.sleep is faster than time.sleep for the same duration
questions.explanation: `asyncio.gather` starts all three coroutines together, and since each one yields control during `await asyncio.sleep(delay)`, their waits overlap — the total time is bounded by the longest single wait, not the sum.

questions.question: Why doesn't declaring a route `async def` automatically make it non-blocking?
options: Because if the code inside it still calls a blocking, synchronous library, that call still blocks the event loop for its full duration
Because FastAPI ignores the async keyword entirely
Because async def routes always run slower than regular def routes
Because async def is only valid for GET requests
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes point out that async only helps when the actual I/O calls inside the function are awaited, async-compatible calls — wrapping a blocking call in an async function doesn't change its blocking behavior.

questions.question: Why is using a background task for work the client actually needs the result of considered a mistake?
options: Because background tasks are always slower than a normal synchronous call
Because it moves the problem — the client ends up polling or guessing when the real result is ready instead of getting it directly in the response
Because background tasks can only be used with GET requests
Because FastAPI does not support background tasks
questions.explanation: If the client genuinely needs the task's output next, firing it as a background task and responding early just defers the client's actual problem rather than solving it.

questions.question: Why doesn't async automatically make a CPU-bound computation faster?
options: Because async specifically helps with I/O-bound waiting, not CPU-bound work, which still blocks the event loop regardless of how the function is declared
Because CPU-bound work is always faster than I/O-bound work already
Because Python cannot execute any CPU-bound code
Because async functions cannot contain any computation at all
questions.explanation: The lesson clarifies that async's benefit comes from yielding control during I/O waits; a slow, CPU-bound calculation has no I/O wait to yield during, so it still blocks the event loop just as it would in a synchronous function.

lessons.title: Request Validation with Pydantic
lessons.description: Catching a malformed request before it ever reaches your business logic — or your LLM API bill.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain why strict request validation matters especially for endpoints that call a paid external API.

sections.title: 🛡️ Validation as a first line of defense
sections.content: Pydantic models validate incoming data's types, required fields, and constraints (string length limits, numeric ranges, allowed enum values) automatically, rejecting malformed requests with a clear error before any application code — including an expensive LLM call — ever executes.

sections.title: 💸 Why this matters more for AI endpoints specifically
sections.content: A malformed request that reaches an LLM call anyway wastes real money on an API call for input that was never going to produce a useful response — validation isn't just about correctness here, it's a cost-control measure directly connected to the LLMOps course's cost-per-token discipline, just applied at the input-validation layer instead of a downstream optimization.

sections.title: 🧩 Nested and custom validation
sections.content: Pydantic supports nested models (a request containing a list of structured objects, not just flat fields) and custom validators for rules that go beyond basic types — like ensuring a prompt field isn't empty, or that a temperature parameter falls within a valid range — encoding business rules directly into the data contract rather than checking them ad hoc inside every endpoint function.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Validating fields for type only, and skipping business-rule constraints.** A `temperature: float` field alone happily accepts `-50.0` or `9999.0` — the type check passes, but the value is still meaningless for an actual LLM call. Custom validators are what catch this class of problem.

**Checking validity after the LLM call instead of before it.** If a request is rejected only after the model has already been called, the cost-control benefit of validation is lost entirely — the point is to reject before the expensive step runs, not after.

**Silently coercing invalid input into something 'close enough' instead of rejecting it.** Clamping an out-of-range temperature to the nearest valid value instead of raising an error hides a bug in whatever sent the invalid value in the first place, and the client never learns their request was malformed.

questions.question: What does Pydantic validation prevent from happening, for a malformed request?
options: It rejects the request with a clear error before any application code, including an LLM call, executes
It silently corrects the request's data without informing the client
It always forwards the request to the LLM regardless of validity
It deletes the malformed request from the server's logs
questions.explanation: Validation acts as a gate that catches problems before they propagate into expensive or incorrect downstream processing.

questions.question: Why does request validation matter more for AI endpoints specifically, compared to a typical CRUD endpoint?
options: Because a malformed request that reaches an LLM call anyway wastes real money on an API call for input that couldn't produce a useful response
Because AI endpoints never receive any invalid requests
Because validation is impossible for endpoints that call an LLM
Because CRUD endpoints have no cost associated with invalid requests either
questions.explanation: The direct dollar cost of an unnecessary LLM API call gives AI endpoints a stronger cost-control reason for strict validation than a typical free CRUD operation.

questions.question: What is an example of a custom validation rule that goes beyond basic type checking?
options: Ensuring a prompt field isn't empty, or that a temperature parameter falls within a valid range
Checking that a request uses the HTTP GET method
Verifying the server's uptime
Confirming the client's IP address is valid
questions.explanation: Custom validators encode specific business rules — like value ranges or non-empty constraints — directly into the data contract, beyond simple type checks.

questions.question: In the code example, what does `validate_and_maybe_call_llm({"prompt": "   ", "temperature": 0.7})` return?
options: "LLM CALLED with prompt='   ', temperature=0.7"
A rejection message, since prompt_not_empty raises a ValueError for a whitespace-only prompt
None
An unhandled crash
questions.explanation: `prompt_not_empty` calls `v.strip()` on the whitespace-only string, which becomes an empty string and fails the `if not v.strip()` check, raising before the LLM would ever be called.

questions.question: Why does `validate_and_maybe_call_llm({"prompt": "Summarize this", "temperature": 5.0})` get rejected?
options: Because the prompt field is empty
Because temperature_in_range rejects 5.0 as outside the valid 0.0 to 2.0 range
Because the prompt is too long
Because CompletionRequest does not accept a temperature field at all
questions.explanation: `temperature_in_range` checks `0.0 <= v <= 2.0`, and 5.0 fails that check, so the ValidationError is raised before any LLM call happens.

questions.question: Why is validating a field's type alone, without a business-rule constraint, called insufficient in the common mistakes?
options: Because a type-only check like temperature: float would still accept clearly invalid values like -50.0 or 9999.0
Because Pydantic cannot check types at all
Because type checks always run slower than custom validators
Because business-rule constraints replace the need for type annotations
questions.explanation: The lesson points out that a bare type annotation passes for any float, including values that are technically the right type but meaningless for an actual LLM call, which is exactly what a custom validator catches.

questions.question: Why does checking validity after the LLM call instead of before it undermine the cost-control benefit?
options: Because if the request is only rejected after the model has already run, the expensive call already happened and the cost was already incurred
Because LLM calls are free regardless of when validation happens
Because validation after the call is technically impossible
Because the order of validation and the LLM call has no effect on cost
questions.explanation: The entire point of validating before the LLM call is to avoid paying for a call on input that will be rejected — validating afterward means the expensive step already ran regardless of the outcome.

questions.question: Why is silently clamping an out-of-range temperature to the nearest valid value instead of rejecting it flagged as a mistake?
options: Because clamping is computationally more expensive than rejecting
Because it hides a bug in whatever sent the invalid value, and the client never learns their request was malformed
Because Pydantic does not support clamping values
Because clamped values always produce worse LLM output than rejected ones
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes note that quietly coercing an invalid value into something 'close enough' masks the underlying problem instead of surfacing it to the client as a clear, actionable error.
